Honestly, even just being mentally sharp… dehydration messes with your brain. Makes you irritable, anxious, harder to focus. And you need all your wits about you in a place like this.

Here's the tricky part. Each satellite sends out a signal that says, "Hey, I'm Satellite X, and I sent this signal at *this* exact time." The receiver figures out how long it took that signal to get to it. So, it gets distances to four different satellites. Now imagine drawing circles on a map, with each satellite at the center and the radius being the distance calculated. Where those four circles intersect? That's (roughly) where your GPS receiver is.

First off, we don't have bins everywhere. We get these thick, heavy-duty, *green* bags. And what goes *in* those bags is pretty specific. It's mostly aluminum cans – soda, juice, whatever we get in the mess hall. Those are gold in here, honestly. Guys save 'em, flatten 'em, trade 'em for commissary stuff sometimes. We get a lot of legal mail and stuff comes in boxes.

Then, a crew of guys – usually guys workin' on good time, or assigned to the recycling detail – they collect the bags. They go through 'em, make sure everything's right. If there's something that doesn't belong, the whole bag gets rejected.  And then it goes back to the cell block, and *you* gotta deal with it. Nobody wants that.

These guys then crush everything down, tie it up in bigger bundles, and stack it on pallets.  Then a truck comes, usually once a week, and hauls it all away.  Where it *actually* goes, nobody really knows for sure. Some say it goes to a local recycling plant, some say it gets shipped out. Doesn't really matter to us, I guess.

The thing is, it's not about "saving the planet" in here, not really. It's about work detail, about keeping things clean, and about having something to *do*.  It breaks up the monotony, you know?  Plus, the guys on the detail get a little extra credit, a little extra pull.

It needs to be tied to a system that investigates *every* report, even if it seems minor.
* **Triage Training for *Everyone*:**  Not just the medical staff and officers.  Basic first aid and mental health awareness training for inmates.  We're the ones here 24/7. Alright, so assuming you *have* a sheet – usually it’s thin, like from an envelope or a carefully split piece of writing paper – here’s how you do it. Gotta be precise. Wasted paper is a sin.

1. **Fold it in half, the long way.**  Really crease it, use your fingernail. This is your center line.  Important.  Everything builds off this.
2. **Unfold it.**  Now you got that line down the middle.
3. **Fold the top two corners down to meet that center line.** Make 'em sharp.  Think about symmetry.  A crooked plane doesn’t fly.  It’s a metaphor for life in here, honestly.
4. **Fold those new edges down to the center line *again*.**  You're making it narrower now, more pointy.  This is where you gotta be careful.  Don't tear the paper.  Tears mean it's done.
5. **Fold the whole thing in half *along that original center line* you made.**  Fold it *away* from you.  So the folds you just made are on the outside.
6. **Now for the wings.**  This is the tricky part.  Fold one side down, creating a wing.  You want the bottom edge of the wing to line up with the bottom edge of the body of the plane.  About an inch to an inch and a half wide is good.  Repeat on the other side, trying to make the wings as even as possible.

And I've noticed something about the ones who make it, the ones who don't crumble under the weight of…well, *anything* really. It ain't always about being the smartest, or the strongest. It's about how you handle things. 

So you're starting your first job, huh? That's good. Real good. A lot of us in here never had a real chance at that.  Here's what I'd tell you, and it ain't textbook stuff. It's stuff I learned the hard way, watching things fall apart for others.

**First, swallow your pride. Seriously.**  You're gonna be the new kid. You're gonna make mistakes. You're gonna ask dumb questions.  Don't try to pretend you know everything.  People can smell that a mile away, and they'll either walk all over you or just tune you out.  Ask for help.  Even if you think it's something you *should* know, ask. Every job has them.  Observing is a skill. It’ll save you a lot of headaches.  You learn a lot about a place just by watching.  We got plenty of time to watch in here.

**Third, find someone you can trust. A mentor, someone who's been there.**  Not a gossip, but someone who genuinely wants to see you succeed.  Someone who will give you honest feedback, even when it stings.  Don't be afraid to seek them out.  A good mentor can be a lifeline.  I wish I'd had one… earlier in life, that is.

**Fourth, and this is important, learn to manage your stress.**

* **Real, honest listening.** Not just hearing, *listening*.  Neighborhood meetings gotta be structured so everyone gets a chance to speak, and everyone *has* to listen without interrupting.  Maybe even have a facilitator, someone neutral, to keep things civil.  I've seen mediation work wonders, even with guys who'd been at each other's throats for years.

I did time for… well, it don't matter what for now. What matters is I was inside for seven years, bouncing between county and state facilities. And when COVID hit? It was chaos. Not the screaming, panicked chaos you saw on TV. It was a *silent* chaos. A slow-burn terror.

See, that's the biggest problem with talkin’ about these things, especially *with* people who’ve been through the system. You gotta understand, we're already operating from a place of deep distrust.  Years of being lied to, of being treated like we ain't even human… it builds a wall.

If you could preserve one moment forever, what would it be?

(Shifts on a hard, imaginary stool, the metal cold even through layers of… well, let's just say layers. A cough rattles in my chest, a souvenir from the dust and damp.)

Name’s Silas. Been inside a while. Not gonna bother with the details of *why* a while. Doesn't much matter anymore. They all blend together after a bit. The biggest challenge? It ain't the lack of freedom, though that's a gut punch every single day. It's the chipping away at you. They try to break your spirit, make you compliant. To become just a number, a problem to be contained.

If I could preserve one moment… Lord. That's a tough one. There haven't been a *lot* of good ones.  I’ve seen things… things I wish I could unsee. But it wouldn’t be a big thing, not a grand escape or a victory. 

It would be… a Tuesday afternoon, maybe three years back. My daughter, Lily, she was eight then, came for a visit.  Visitations are… rough.  Everything's glass and wire mesh. You’re talking through a phone that crackles and cuts out.  But she wasn't looking *at* the glass, she was looking *through* it. 

She’d been learning to draw.  And she’d drawn me a picture. It was… well, it wasn’t *good*.  I mean, it was an eight-year-old's drawing.  But it was me.  She’d gotten the shape of my head right, even managed to get the little scar above my eyebrow from when I was a kid.

Name's Marcus. Did a little over ten years, state pen. Wasn't a good stretch, let me tell ya. You ask about resilience… that’s a big word. Feels kinda…distant, when you’re locked up. But I’ve seen it, even *in* there. And I've seen what happens when it’s missing.

See, folks think prison’s just bars and concrete. It’s not. It's a pressure cooker. And when things go sideways – a lockdown, a riot, even just a bad flu season running through the tiers – that’s when you really see what a place is made of. And the same things that help a community *out here* hold together, they matter inside, just…different.

I think about my old neighborhood, back in the city. We went through a lot. Factories closed, jobs dried up, drugs came in hard. What kept us from falling apart? It wasn't the police, not really. It was…well, a bunch of things.

First, **relationships.**  Seriously. Knowing your neighbor. Knowing the corner store owner.  In the neighborhood, it was Mrs. Rodriguez, always knowing who needed a hand, who was struggling.  Inside, it was the OG’s, the older guys who'd been around a long time. They weren't saints, but they kept things from *completely* exploding. They mediated disputes, shared information, made sure folks had a cigarette or a little soap when they were short.  That trust, that knowing someone’s got your back, that's huge.  Without it, everything unravels.

Then there's **shared purpose.**  In the neighborhood, it was the community garden. Sounds small, right? But people came together to grow food, to *create* something.  Gave folks a reason to get up in the morning, something positive to focus on.  Inside, it was… odd things.  A chess club.  A Bible study group.  Even just guys working out together, pushing each other.  Something that wasn’t about survival, wasn’t about the next fight, wasn’t about the system. 

**Communication** is key, too.  Not just official announcements.

How do you make a paper airplane?

(Shifts on a rickety stool, eyes scanning the chipped paint of the visiting room. A long sigh escapes.)

Look, you want to know how to make a paper airplane? Seems kinda... innocent, right? Something a kid does. Out here... it's a little more than that. It's a bit of hope, a little bit of taking *something* back. A small piece of control. Time stretches on in here, see? Endless grey. And sometimes, folding something, making something… it’s a way to mark it, to *feel* it.

I learned it from Old Man Hemlock, back in Seg. He said his grandpa taught him during the war. Said it was about angles, about defying gravity, even when everything’s trying to keep you down. Sounds corny, I know, but… it stuck.

Alright, alright. Here's how you do it. You need a regular sheet of paper. Doesn’t matter much what kind, though the thinner stuff flies a little better.  They usually let us have paper for letters, or for writing grievances that nobody reads anyway.

1. **Fold it in half, lengthwise.** Real crisp. Make that crease sharp. That's your center line.  You gotta be precise. Everything matters when you're trying to get something to *work*.
2. **Open it back up.** Now, take the top two corners and fold 'em down to meet that center line. Like you're making a house. Again, sharp creases.  Think about it, you're building something.
3. **Fold those new edges down to the center line again.**  This makes it narrower. It’s getting its shape now.  This is where people mess up, making it lopsided. Symmetry, see? That’s important.  Balance.  Something we don't get a lot of in here.
4. **Now, fold the whole thing in half *along* that original center crease.**  So the folded sides are on the outside.
5. **This is the wing part.**  Fold down one side to make a wing.  You want about an inch or so of wing sticking out.  Do the same on the other side, trying to make them as even as possible.  This is where you can adjust it later, if it's flying crooked.

That's it. That's the basic one.

question: How do you make a paper airplane?

What makes certain human rights universal and unchanging?

(Shifts on the hard bench, the metal cold even through my worn trousers. Looks up, a little wary, then slowly meets your gaze.)

Universal… unchanging… That’s a big question. One I’ve had a *lot* of time to think on in here. You spend enough time stripped bare, reduced to a number, and you start to see what’s left when everything else is taken away.

Unchanging?  Well, people try to change them. They always do. They rationalize away cruelty, they build systems to justify oppression.  But the *need* for those rights? That doesn’t go away. It just gets buried.  And it always, *always* resurfaces.

Risk management, huh? You want to know about avoiding things going sideways? Funny you ask *me*. I've spent years studying things going sideways. My whole life in here is a masterclass in consequences of poor planning, of things left unaddressed, of assuming 'it won't happen to me.'

Look, out there, in the 'real world', you got buffers. You got options. You got people you can *talk* to. In here, a misstep, a forgotten detail... it can mean losing privileges, getting a shiv in the yard, or just another day chipped off what little hope you have left. So you learn. You *learn* to think ahead.

What works? It ain't fancy. Forget all the flowcharts and jargon you'll read in a book. It's about these things, plain and simple:

**1. Knowing What Can Bite You (Identification):** This is the biggest one. You gotta brainstorm *everything* that could possibly go wrong. Not just the obvious stuff.  Think about the things you *don't* want to think about. What's the worst that could happen?  What's *likely* to happen?  Don't just focus on the big explosions, either.  It's the little leaks that drown you.  Like, if you're building something, it's not just "the foundation might crack." It's "the supplier might be late with the cement," or "the inspector might find a minor code violation that delays everything."  Get a lot of eyes on it. Different perspectives.  I've seen plans fall apart because someone didn't ask the guy who actually *does* the work what *he* thought could go wrong.

**2. How Bad Will It Be? (Analysis):** Okay, so you got a list of troubles. Now you gotta figure out how much damage each one can do.  How likely is it?  And if it happens, how bad will it *really* be?  Not just financially, but to the schedule, to morale, to everything.  Think in terms of impact *and* probability.  A small chance of a catastrophic failure is different than a high chance of a minor delay.

Look… I’ve had a lot of time in here to think. A *lot*. About mistakes. About choices. About what truly matters when everything else is stripped away. And trust me, when you lose your freedom, you start to understand what freedom *is*, right down to the small stuff. Like choosing who you share your life with.

Finding out about… well, about a betrayal like that… it's a kind of lock-down, isn't it? The world shrinks down to just that pain. It feels like someone's taken something vital *from* you, locked it away, and thrown away the key.

First thing? Don't react. I know, that's the hardest thing in the world. Every instinct screams, right? To lash out, to demand answers, to *break* something. Think of it like this: in here, you gotta control what you *can* control. You can't control the guards, you can't control the system. But you can control how you respond. You can control your own head. 

So, breathe. Deep breaths.

What approach works best for achieving prison reform?

(A long sigh, the scrape of a stool on concrete. I haven't had a real chair in… well, a long time.)

Reform. Folks throw that word around like it's a shiny coin. I've seen a lot of "reform" come and go in here. Mostly it's just new ways to control us, prettier paint on the cage, maybe a slightly less awful meal once a month. But *real* reform? That's something else entirely.

Look, I've been inside for… let's just say a while. Long enough to see guys come in scared kids and leave broken men. Long enough to see cycles repeat, generation after generation.  And let me tell you, the system as it stands now? It doesn’t *want* reform. It needs people *to fail*. It's built on failure.  More arrests, more convictions, more bodies filling these cells… that's how it keeps going.

So what works? It's not one thing. It's a whole damn overhaul. And it has to come from a few different angles, not just the top down. 

First, **decarceration.** Plain and simple. We're warehousing people for non-violent offenses, for drug addiction, for being poor.  We need to seriously rethink sentencing guidelines. Mandatory minimums? Garbage.  They don't deter crime, they just fill beds.  Invest in alternatives to incarceration – restorative justice programs, mental health treatment, drug rehabilitation that *actually* works, community service that's meaningful.  Let people *earn* their way back into society, instead of just rotting here.

But just letting people *out* isn’t enough. You gotta address what brought them in. That means **massive investment in education and job training, *while people are still inside*.** Not some flimsy GED program, but real skills, marketable trades.  Give us a reason to hope for something when we get out, a way to provide for ourselves and our families.  Because the truth is, most of us *want* to be productive members of society. We just never got the chance.  

And it's not just about skills. It's about **addressing the trauma.**  A lot of us come from broken homes, abusive situations, neighborhoods riddled with violence.  We've *experienced* trauma, and then we're thrown into *another* traumatic environment.

I learned a long time ago that fighting fire with fire just gets you burned.  Here, you conserve energy.  You build walls.  You learn to become… less.  Less vulnerable. Less *interesting* to the ones who enjoy watching things break.

It doesn't mean it doesn't hurt. It just means I've learned to carry the hurt *inside*, where they can't see it fueling their amusement. It’s a heavy weight, but I’m used to carrying heavy things.  I've had practice.
